```{r echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# Load functions in env

knn_plot <- function(w, k) {
  cow_n <- knn_tibble(w, k)
  avg <- cow_n |>
    filter(neighbor == 1) %>%
    .$fat %>%
    mean()

  p <-
    knn_tibble(w, k) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(week, fat, color = neighbor), size = 3) +
    # labs(y = "Fat Content (%)") +
    ggtitle(paste("k = ", k)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = w, alpha = 0.35) +
    annotate("point", x = w, y = avg, shape = 18, fill = "black", size = 4.5) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 19, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 17),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 18),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 18, margin = margin(r = 1, unit = "cm")), 
    legend.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"))

  return(p)
}

knn_tibble <- function(w, k){
  ## beaware that the way we handle ties here might differ.
    
  fat_content2 <- 
    fat_content |>
    mutate(neighbor = w) |>
    mutate(neighbor = row_number(abs(neighbor - week))) |>
    mutate(neighbor = as_factor(if_else(neighbor > k, true = 0, false = 1)))
    
  return(fat_content2)    
}
```

## Today's Learning Goals

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- Define the concept of <span style="color: purple;">local regression</span>.
- Model and perform <span style="color: purple;">piecewise constant, linear, and continuous linear</span> local regressions.
- Extend the concept of <span style="color: purple;">$k$-NN classification to a regression framework</span>.
- Define and apply <span style="color: purple;">locally weighted scatterplot smoother regression</span>.

## It is time to...

Put aside regression techniques on the global conditioned mean and check local alternatives  <span style="color: purple;">suitable for predictions</span>!

<br>

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="300" height="300"/>
</center>

## 1. Piecewise Local Regression

- Retaking our <span style="color: purple;">initial motivation</span> in this course, the classical linear regression model (Ordinary Least-squares, OLS) is focused on the conditional mean on the regressors:

::: {.small-text}
$$
\mathbb{E}(Y_i \mid X_{i,j} = x_{i,j}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i,1} + \ldots + \beta_k x_{i,k} \; \; \; \; \text{since} \; \; \; \; \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0.
$$
:::

- We already stated that a model of this class, i.e. parametric, favours <span style="color: purple;">interpretability</span> when we aim to make inference on the response and regressors.

### Nonetheless...

- Suppose our goal is an <span style="color: purple;">accurate prediction</span> in many complex frameworks (e.g., non-linear). 
- In that case, the global linearity in models such as the OLS case is not that flexible.
- Therefore, we can use <span style="color: purple;">local regression techniques</span>.

<center>        
<img src="images/bulb.png" width="180" height="225"/>
</center>

### 1.1. Piecewise Constant Regression

- This regression technique is based on fitting different <span style="color: purple;">local OLS regressions</span>. 
- The <span style="color: purple;">step function</span> is the key concept here.
- The idea behind the <span style="color: purple;">step function</span> is to break the range of the regressor into intervals. 
- In each interval, we adjust a <span style="color: purple;">constant</span>. We obtain the average response in that interval.

### Example

- Let us take the 2-$d$ framework. For the $i$th observation in the sample, suppose we have a respose $Y_i$ subject to a regressor $X_i$.
- Instead of making a <span style="color: purple;">global parametric assumption</spasn>, we break the range of the regressor into $q$ <span style="color: purple;">knots</span> $c_1, c_2, \dots, c_q$. 
- Hence, the regressor will be sectioned <span style="color: purple;">in bins changing from continuous to categorical</span>.

### The step functions

::: {.small-text-v2}
- The step functions are merely <span style="color: purple;">dummy variables</span>.

\begin{equation*}
C_0(X_i) = I(X_i < c_1) =
\begin{cases}
1 \; \; \; \; \mbox{if $X_i < c_1$},\\
0 \; \; \; \; 	\mbox{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
C_1(X_i) = I(c_1 \leq X_i < c_2) =
\begin{cases}
1 \; \; \; \; \mbox{if $c_1 \leq X_i < c_2$},\\
0 \; \; \; \; 	\mbox{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}

$$\vdots$$

\begin{equation*}
C_{q -1 }(X_i) = I(c_{q - 1} \leq X_i < c_q) =
\begin{cases}
1 \; \; \; \; \mbox{if $c_{q-1} \leq X_i < c_q$},\\
0 \; \; \; \; 	\mbox{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
C_q(X_i) = I(c_q \leq X_i) =
\begin{cases}
1 \; \; \; \; \mbox{if $c_q \leq X_i$},\\
0 \; \; \; \; 	\mbox{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
:::

### Then...

::: {.small-text}

- We run an OLS model based on these previous step functions <span style="color: purple;">and not the continuous $X_i$</span>.
- The regression model becomes
$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 C_1(X_i) + \beta_2 C_2(X_i) + \dots + \beta_{q-1} C_{q-1}(X_i) + \beta_q C_q(X_i) + \varepsilon_i.
$$
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
> **Heads-up:** The step function $C_0(X_i)$ does not appear in the model given that $\beta_0$ can be interpreted as the response's mean when $X_i < c_1$ (i.e., the rest of the $q$ step functions are equal to zero).
:::

### Cow Milk Dataset

- We will use this dataset provided by [Henderson and McCulloch (1990)](https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/handle/1813/31620/BU-1049-MA.pdf;jsessionid=1E54532D482EC351824111A78C797021?sequence=1). 
- The <span style="color: purple;">whole dataset</span> contains the average daily milk `fat` yields from a cow in kg/day, from `week` 1 to 35.

<center>        
<img src="images/cow.png" width="180" height="200"/>
</center>

### Piecewise constant regression

- Let us fit a piecewise constant regression with $q = 4$ knots.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# Define the number of step functions (q + 1)
breaks_q <- 5

# Create the steps for week.
fat_content <- fat_content |>
  mutate(steps = cut(fat_content$week, breaks = breaks_q, right = FALSE))

# Checking levels in steps
levels(fat_content$steps)
```

### New column added!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
head(fat_content)
tail(fat_content)
```

### Fit the model!

::: {.small-text}
- We can now fit the `model_steps` with `formula = fat ~ steps` via `lm()`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
model_steps <- lm(formula = fat ~ steps, data = fat_content)
tidy(model_steps) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

> **Heads-up:** Note that `estimate` is the difference between each category with respect to the baseline `[0.966,7.8)`.
:::

### Glancing at the model!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(model_steps) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
 breaks_q <- 5

fat_content <- fat_content |>
  mutate(steps = cut(fat_content$week, breaks = breaks_q, right = FALSE))

model_steps <- lm(formula = fat ~ steps, data = fat_content)

# Creating the grid for predictions.
grid <- fat_content |>
  data_grid(week = seq_range(week, 1000)) |>
  mutate(steps = cut(week, breaks_q, right = FALSE)) |>
  add_predictions(model_steps)

# Creating labels and plotting values for the knots.
labs <- levels(fat_content$steps)
steps <- tibble(
  lower = as.numeric(sub("\\[(.+),.*", "\\1", labs)),
  upper = as.numeric(sub("[^,]*,([^]]*)\\)", "\\1", labs))
)
```

### Plotting

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 15
#| fig.height: 8

plot_cow +
  geom_line(aes(week, pred), data = grid, color = "blue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = steps$lower[-1], linetype = "dashed")  +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 35), breaks = seq(0, 35, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.8), breaks = seq(0, 0.8, by = 0.2))
```

### 1.2. Non-Continuous Piecewise Linear Regression

::: {.small-text}
- Note in the previous plot, though, that the functions should not be constant inside an interval. 
- Instead, <span style="color: purple;">there is an approximately linear behaviour in each interval</span>.
- <span style="color: purple;">Can we capture that? Yes we can!</span>
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
- All we need to do, is to add $\color{green}{\text{interaction terms}}$ between the step functions $C_j(X_i)$, for $j = 1, \dots, q$, with $X_i$:
\begin{equation*}
Y_i = \beta_0 + \color{red}{\beta_1 C_1(X_i) + \dots + \beta_q C_q(X_i)} + \beta_{q + 1} X_i + \\ \color{green}{\beta_{q + 2} X_i C_1(X_i) + \dots + \beta_{2q + 1} X_i C_q(X_i)} + \varepsilon_i.
\end{equation*}
:::

### Hence...

::: {.small-text}
- Let us see what happens in this model:

- If $X_i < c_1$, then our model is: $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{q + 1}X_i$
- If $c_1 \leq X_i < c_2$, then our model is: $Y_i = \beta_0 + \color{red}{\beta_1} + (\beta_{q + 1} + \color{green}{\beta_{q + 2}}) X_i$
- If $c_2 \leq X_i < c_3$, then our model is: $Y_i = \beta_0 + \color{red}{\beta_2} + (\beta_{q + 1} + \color{green}{\beta_{q + 3}}) X_i$

$$\vdots$$

- If $c_{q-1} \leq X_i < c_q$, then our model is: $Y_i = \beta_0 + \color{red}{\beta_{q -1}} + (\beta_{q + 1} + \color{green}{\beta_{2q}}) X_i$
- If $c_q \leq X_i$, then our model is: $Y_i = \beta_0 + \color{red}{\beta_q} + (\beta_{q + 1} + \color{green}{\beta_{2q + 1}}) X_i$
:::

### Additional terms!

- So, for each interval, we have an $\color{red}{\text{additional intercept}}$ and an $\color{green}{\text{additional slope}}$.

- Now, we will check if the model fitting looks better in `fat_content`. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# We need to add the interaction between steps and week.
model_piecewise_linear <- lm(formula = fat ~ week * steps, data = fat_content)
```

- Note that the right hand side in the `formula`, within `lm()`, is merely a model with interaction `week * steps`.

### Plot in `R`!

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 15
#| fig.height: 8

# We need to add the interaction between steps and week.
model_piecewise_linear <- lm(fat ~ week * steps, data = fat_content)

## Let us create our grid for predictions,
grid <- fat_content |>
  data_grid(week = seq_range(week, 1000)) |>
  mutate(steps = cut(week, breaks_q, right = FALSE)) |>
  add_predictions(model_piecewise_linear)

plot_cow +
  geom_line(aes(week, pred), data = grid, color = "blue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = steps$lower[-1], alpha = 1, linetype = "dashed")
```

### Model summary!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
tidy(model_piecewise_linear) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

### Glancing at the model!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(model_piecewise_linear) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

### However...

The local regression lines are disconnected!

> Can we fix that?

<center>
<img src="images/panda.png" width="300" height="300"/>
</center>

### 1.3. Continuous Piecewise Linear Regression

::: {.small-text}
- We can impose <span style="color: purple;">restrictions</span> to make sure that the lines are connected to each other. 
- Therefore, we need to introduce the concept of the <span style="color: purple;">hinge function</span>.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
- For the $i$th observation, this model can be defined as follows:
$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i +\beta_2 (X_i - c_1)_{+} + \dots + \beta_{q+1} (X_i - c_q)_{+} + \varepsilon_i.$$
- The hinge function for the knot $c_j$ is:
$$
(X_i - c_j)_{+} =
\begin{cases}
0 \; \; \; \; \mbox{if $X_i < c_j$},\\
X_i - c_j \; \; \; \;   \mbox{if $X_i \geq c_j$}.
\end{cases}
$$
:::

### One line more!

- We do not need to fit separate OLS linear regressions but rather one. 
- In the `lm()` function, within `formula` on the right-hand side along with the standalone regressor `X`, we have to add up the following term: 

`I((X - c_j)*(X >= c_j))` <span style="color: purple;">by knot `c_j`</span>.

<center>        
<img src="images/bulb.png" width="90" height="112.5"/>
</center>

### Fitting the Model

::: {.small-text}
- We need to obtain the corresponding knots in `fat_content` ($q = 4$) and, then, use `lm()`.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
levels(fat_content$steps)
knots <- c(7.8, 14.6, 21.4, 28.2)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
model_piecewise_cont_linear <- lm(
  fat ~ week +
    I((week - knots[1]) * (week >= knots[1])) +
    I((week - knots[2]) * (week >= knots[2])) +
    I((week - knots[3]) * (week >= knots[3])) +
    I((week - knots[4]) * (week >= knots[4])),
  data = fat_content
)
```

### Prediction grid!

- Now, we will check if the model predictions look better in `fat_content`.
- Let us create our grid for predictions.
- We use the same functions as in the previous two models (one grid per model).

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
grid <- fat_content |>
  data_grid(week = seq_range(week, 1000)) |>
  mutate(steps = cut(week, breaks_q, right = FALSE)) |>
  add_predictions(model_piecewise_cont_linear)

```

### Adding plotting layer!

- We also include the vertical dashed lines.

```{webr}
labs <- levels(fat_content$steps)
steps <- tibble(
  lower = as.numeric(sub("\\[(.+),.*", "\\1", labs)),
  upper = as.numeric(sub("[^,]*,([^]]*)\\)", "\\1", labs))
)
  
plot_cow +
  geom_line(aes(week, pred), data = grid, color = "blue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = steps$lower[-1], alpha = 1, linetype = "dashed")
```

### Plotting!

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 15
#| fig.height: 8

knots <- c(7.8, 14.6, 21.4, 28.2)

model_piecewise_cont_linear <- lm(fat ~ week + I((week - knots[1]) * (week >= knots[1])) +
  I((week - knots[2]) * (week >= knots[2])) +
  I((week - knots[3]) * (week >= knots[3]))+
  I((week - knots[4]) * (week >= knots[4])),
data = fat_content
)

grid <- fat_content |>
  data_grid(week = seq_range(week, 1000))  |>
  mutate(steps = cut(week, breaks_q, right = FALSE)) |>
  add_predictions(model_piecewise_cont_linear)

plot_cow +
  geom_line(aes(week, pred), data = grid, color = "blue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = steps$lower[-1], alpha = 1, linetype = "dashed")
```


### Model's Summary

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
tidy(model_piecewise_cont_linear) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
glance(model_piecewise_cont_linear) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

## 2. $k$-NN Regression

::: {.small-text}

> **Heads-up:** We have been using the letter $k$ to denote the number of regressors in any regression model. Nevertheless, this letter is reserved for groups of $k$ observations in this framework. Therefore, we will switch to the letter $p$ to denote the number  regressors in this framework.

:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}

- The idea behind $k$-NN regression is finding the $k$ observations <span style="color: purple;">in our training dataset of size $n$ (with $p$ features $x_j$ per observation)</span> closest to the new point we want to predict. 
- Next, we calculate the average $\bar{y}^{(k)}$ of the responses of those $k$ observations. That is our new prediction.
:::


### How do we obtain those $k$ observations? 

- <span style="color: purple;">Based on the values of the respective $p$ features</span>, we determine which $k$ observations (out from the $n$ in the training set) have the smallest distance metric (e.g., Euclidean distance $D^{(\text{Training, New})}$) to the <span style="color: purple;">features of the new point</span>.

$$
D^{(\text{Training, New})} = \sqrt{\sum_{j = 1}^p \Big( x_j^{\text{(Training)}} - x_j^{\text{(New)}} \Big)^2}
$$

### Things to keep in mind!

1. If $k = 1$, there will be <span style="color: purple;">no training error</span>. Nevertheless, <span style="color: purple;">we might (and probably will) overfit badly</span>. 
2. As we increase $k$, more <span style="color: purple;">"smooth"</span> the regression will be. At some point, <span style="color: purple;">we will start underfitting</span>.

- Now let us run $k$-NN algorithm on the `fat_content` dataset.

### Plots!

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 20
#| fig.height: 10

# Use odd numbers here so there is no missmatch on how the ties are handled.
k <- 3

## Running k-NN regression
my_knn <- knnreg(fat ~ week, data = fat_content, k = k)

grid <- fat_content |>
  data_grid(week) |>
  add_predictions(my_knn)

## Generating the plots.
p <- list()
for (i in 1:6) {
  p[[i]] <- knn_plot((i - 1) * 7 + 1, k) + geom_line(aes(week, pred), data = grid)
}

grid.arrange(grobs = p, ncol = 2)
```

### iClicker Question

What are the consequences of <span style="color: purple;">overfitting</span> a training set in further test sets?

**A.** There are no consequences at all; <span style="color: purple;">predictions will be highly accurate in any further test set</span>.

**B.** The trained model will be so oversimplified that <span style="color: purple;">we will have a high bias in further test set predictions</span>.

**C.** The trained model will be so overfitted that <span style="color: purple;">it will also explain random noise in training data</span>. Therefore, we cannot generalize this model in further test set predictions.

## 3. Locally Weighted Scatterplot Smoother (LOWESS) Regression

:::: {.small-text}
::: {.incremental}
- Suppose we want to predict the response $y$ for a given $x$. For example, we want to predict the fat content of cow milk in `week` 10. 
- The idea of LOWESS is:
  1. Find the closest points to `week` 10 (<span style="color: purple;">how many points is a parameter that we define</span>).
  2. From the selected points, we assign <span style="color: purple;">weights</span> based on these distances. The closest the point is, the more weight it will receive (weights are determined as in <span style="color: purple;">Weighted Least-squares (WLS)</span> by default in `loess()`).
:::
::::

### Cont'd

::: {.small-text}
3. Next, for the $i$th point in the `span`, using WLS for a <span style="color: purple;">second `degree` polynomial</span> for instance, we minimize the sum of squared errors considering the weight $w_i$ as follows:
   \begin{equation*}
\sum_i w_i \left(y_i - \beta_0-\beta_1 x_i-\beta_2 x_i^2\right)^2
\end{equation*}

> **Heads-up:** Roughly speaking, WLS is used when the error variance differs across observations. If $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid x_i) = \sigma_i^2$, then (up to a constant factor) the standard choice is $w_i \propto 1/\sigma_i^2$. Using these weights can improve efficiency and helps model heteroscedasticity.
:::

### 

Now, there are a couple of things to consider in `loess()`: 

- The parameter `span` (between `0` and `1`) defines the "*size*" of your neighbourhood. To be more exact, it specifies the proportion of points considered as neighbours of $x$. <span style="color: purple;">The higher the proportion, the smoother the fitted surface will be.</span>
- The parameter `degree`, specifies if you are fitting a constant (`degree`= 0), a linear model (`degree` = 1), or a quadratic model (`degree` = 2). By quadratic, we mean $\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i+\beta_2 x_i^2$.

###

```{r}
#| echo: false

p <- list()
i <- 1
for (degree in seq(0, 2, 1)) {
  for (span in seq(0.25, 1, 0.25)) {
    
    suppressWarnings(model_loess <- loess(fat ~ week, span = span, degree = degree, data = fat_content))

    # We create our grid for predictions.
    grid <- fat_content |>
      data_grid(week = seq_range(week, 1000)) |>
      add_predictions(model_loess)

    # Plotting.
    p[[i]] <- plot_cow +
      geom_line(aes(week, pred), data = grid, color = "red") +
      theme(
        plot.title = element_text(size = 24),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 18)
      ) +
      ggtitle(paste0("degree = ", degree, "  span = ", span))

    i <- i + 1
  }
}

```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 20
#| fig.height: 10
grid.arrange(grobs = p[1:6], ncol = 2)
```

###

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 20
#| fig.height: 10
grid.arrange(grobs = p[7:12], ncol = 2)
```


## 4. Wrapping Up

- Local regression is a great tool for addressing <span style="color: purple;">predictive inquiries</span>.
- Nonetheless, we will lose our <span style="color: purple;">inferential interpretability</span>.
- The key concept in local regression techniques is <span style="color: purple;">"*how local we want our model to be*."</span>
